book_title: Chapter 3: Inside the Value Chain — NIKE Direct vs. Wholesale, Asian Sourcing & Unit Economics
question: How does Nike convert a $30 contract-manufactured sneaker into $46.4 billion of global revenue, and why did the shift between Wholesale and NIKE Direct reshape its unit economics?

epigraph.quote: Distribution is not a zero-sum channel war; wholesale builds the consumer habit and discovery funnel, while direct captures the highest-intent repeat buyer.
epigraph.author: Chapter 3 Supply Chain & Unit Economics Synthesis

web_blocks.title: 3.1 The Channel Rebalance: Wholesale ($27.5B) vs. NIKE Direct ($17.7B)

web_blocks.html: Nike sells its products through two primary channels: Wholesale and NIKE Direct [1, 2]. Wholesale covers multi-brand chains like Dick's Sporting Goods, Foot Locker, and JD Sports, plus specialty run shops and global distributors [1, 2]. NIKE Direct spans Nike-owned flagship and outlet stores alongside Nike.com and the Nike/SNKRS apps [1, 2]. Under John Donahoe's Consumer Direct Acceleration (2020–2024), management targeted a 50% digital mix (40% owned digital) by FY2025 and cut roughly half of its wholesale accounts [13]. On paper, selling direct captures ~100% of retail MSRP rather than ~50% wholesale price, lifting gross margin.

In practice, unit economics turned far harsher once organic traffic cooled. Digital fulfillment carries steep variable costs inside Cost of Sales and Operating Overhead, including single-parcel shipping, free-return logistics, paid marketing, and app upkeep. Leaving multi-brand stores also starved Nike of top-of-funnel shopper discovery. That forced heavier markdowns on Nike.com and in factory outlets to clear excess stock. Under Elliott Hill's 'Win Now' reset, Wholesale rebounded to $27,515 million in FY2026 (~59% of consolidated revenue, up ~6% YoY), while NIKE Direct fell to $17,692 million (~38% of revenue) [2, 4]. That gap widened in Q1 FY2027: NIKE Brand Wholesale held firm at $6.8 billion (-1% globally, +9% in North America), while NIKE Direct dropped 8% to $4.14 billion (Digital -13%, owned stores -5%) [3, 21].

Nike owns zero footwear factories. In FY2026, independent contract plants across 11 countries made 100% of NIKE Brand footwear [1, 12]. Just three countries—Vietnam (52%), Indonesia (27%), and China (16%)—supplied 95% of total footwear volume [1, 12]. Four major contract manufacturing groups alone produced roughly 60% of total pairs [1]. Apparel production is similarly outsourced across Vietnam, China, Cambodia, and other hubs. This asset-light model keeps capital spending remarkably low at $684 million in FY2026, or 1.5% of revenue [1, 20]. At the same time, it concentrates trade and tariff risk in Southeast Asia and China.

Tariff swings directly whipsawed Nike's FY2026 P&L. Higher product and duty costs weighed on baseline gross margins throughout the year. In Q4 FY2026, however, Nike booked a $986 million benefit ($965 million in North America, $21 million in Converse) from expected recovery of IEEPA tariffs paid on U.S. imports [1, 2]. Looking ahead, management launched the 'Pace' operating transformation in October 2026. The plan aims to boost supply-chain speed, merge regional units into three geographies, and capture $2.5 billion in annualized run-rate structural savings by FY2031 [7].

Beyond footwear factories, FY2026 Form 10-K and Q1 FY2027 Form 10-Q footnotes highlight three underappreciated supply-chain and regulatory exposures [36, 37]. First, apparel and material supplier concentration mirrors footwear: 64 contract manufacturers operated 321 finished-goods apparel plants across 34 countries in FY2026, with Vietnam (34%), Cambodia (15%), and China (12%) supplying 61% of volume and the top six manufacturers producing ~54% (two exceeding 10% each), supported by 205 strategic Tier-2 material suppliers and internal Air Manufacturing Innovation facilities (Beaverton, St. Charles, and Dong Nai City, Vietnam) for Air-Sole components [1, 37]. Conversely, customer concentration is well diversified, with no single wholesale account exceeding 10% of consolidated revenue in FY2026, while $1.1 billion of confirmed supplier obligations ($11.5 billion annual invoice volume) sit inside voluntary supplier finance programs within Accounts Payable [1, 37]. Second, on tariff cash timing and litigation, Nike collected substantially all of the remaining $684 million IEEPA tariff receivable during Q1 FY2027 (following $302 million received by May 31, 2026), yet Note 11 of the Q1 FY2027 10-Q flags an unresolved Belgian Customs duty appeal covering imports since FY2018—backed by bank guarantees, with an unestimable potential material adverse loss [37]. Third, Note 10 discloses that Nike assigns standard foreign-currency rates twice yearly to geographic segments while absorbing rate variances and derivative hedge gains or losses centrally in Corporate, creating recurring FX noise between regional and consolidated margins [37].

Because demand creation ($4,754 million) and operating overhead ($11,360 million) stay largely fixed in the near term, modest revenue drops sharply squeeze operating profit and cash conversion [1, 20].

book_paragraphs: If you want to see why Nike's margin profile changed so dramatically over the last five years, you and I need to trace a single sneaker from a factory floor in Ho Chi Minh City to a customer's doorstep. Nike is a masterclass in asset-light manufacturing: it owns zero footwear factories. Instead, four giant contract-manufacturing groups build roughly 60% of its footwear, and three countries—Vietnam at 52%, Indonesia at 27%, and China at 16%—supply 95% of total footwear pairs. Apparel follows a parallel playbook across 321 factories and 64 manufacturers, with Vietnam (34%), Cambodia (15%), and China (12%) dominating and the top six apparel vendors supplying roughly 54%, alongside 205 strategic Tier-2 raw-material suppliers and Nike's own Air Manufacturing Innovation plants supplying proprietary Air-Soles. Meanwhile, wholesale customer concentration remains low—no single customer accounted for 10% or more of FY2026 consolidated sales—while $1.1 billion of supplier invoices flow through voluntary supplier finance programs. Because partners carry the factory depreciation, Nike only had to spend $684 million on capital expenditures in FY2026 on a $46.4 billion business, or 1.5% of revenue.

So where did the margin leakage happen? It happened in the last mile of distribution. During the Consumer Direct Acceleration boom, management fell in love with a spreadsheet illusion: if you sell a $140 shoe on Nike.com instead of selling it to Dick's Sporting Goods for $75 wholesale, you capture double the revenue and pocket the retail markup. What the spreadsheet underweighted was the cost of single-parcel shipping, free-return logistics, paid digital acquisition, and the brand tax of disappearing from physical multi-brand shelves. When traffic slowed, Nike had to discount on its own website and in its own outlet stores, eroding both gross margin and brand prestige.

Watch what happened in FY2026 when Elliott Hill reversed course. Wholesale climbed back to $27.52 billion—roughly 59% of the business—while NIKE Direct shrank to $17.69 billion, or 38%. In Q1 FY2027, North America wholesale grew 9% while NIKE Brand Digital fell 13%. That is not a sign of failure; it is a deliberate detox from low-quality, promotional digital volume back toward full-price wholesale partnerships.

Look closely at the FY2026 dollar waterfall we built from the 10-K. Out of $46,398 million in revenue, Cost of Sales consumed $26,487 million, leaving $19,911 million in gross profit (42.9%). Then Demand Creation—the athlete contracts and global ad campaigns—took $4,754 million, and Operating Overhead—store leases, corporate payroll, IT, and logistics—took $11,360 million (including $747 million of depreciation). That left $3,797 million in operating income, or an 8.2% operating margin. After $103 million of net interest and other income and $792 million of taxes, Net Income landed at $3,108 million. Yet because of working-capital timing, Cash Provided by Operations was only $2,868 million, leaving $2,184 million of Free Cash Flow after $684 million of CapEx. For a company that once converted over 12% of sales into cash, a 4.7% FCF margin explains why Dave Denton immediately launched the 'Pace' program to strip out $2.5 billion of structural costs.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Asset-light manufacturing makes Nike look like a software-adjacent royalty business at the factory gate, but owned retail stores and single-parcel e-commerce reintroduce heavy fixed and fulfillment costs at the doorstep.

book_subsections.title: The 'Pace' Supply-Chain Overhaul and Tariff Mechanics
paragraphs: You also have to understand why tariffs, customs disputes, and factory concentration sit at the center of Nike's unit-economics debate right now. With 52% of footwear and 34% of apparel built in Vietnam, 27% of footwear in Indonesia, and 16% of footwear in China, any shift in U.S. reciprocal tariff schedules hits landed cost of goods immediately. In FY2026, higher product and duty costs weighed on baseline margins, even though Q4 benefited from $986 million in one-time IEEPA tariff recovery bookings ($965 million in North America and $21 million in Converse)—of which $302 million was collected by May 31, 2026 and substantially all of the remaining $684 million receivable was collected in cash during Q1 FY2027. Yet regulatory friction is not over: Q1 FY2027 Form 10-Q Note 11 discloses an ongoing Belgian Customs appellate claim over alleged underpaid duties dating back to FY2018 imports, backed by bank guarantees with an unestimable potential material adverse outcome, while twice-yearly internal standard FX rates route currency hedge and conversion swings into Corporate.

That is the operational backdrop for the 'Pace' transformation unveiled by Elliott Hill and CFO Dave Denton in October 2026. Rather than merely trimming corporate headcount, Pace targets $2.5 billion in annualized run-rate structural savings through FY2031 by modernizing end-to-end supply-chain planning, collapsing four regional operating silos into three streamlined geographies (Americas, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific/Greater China), and scaling new operational hubs such as Bengaluru, India. If Pace succeeds in shortening factory-to-shelf lead times, Nike can order closer to real-time demand—reducing the working-capital trap that dragged operating cash flow down to $2.87 billion in FY2026.

book_subsections.title: Inside the Contract Factory Gate and the Last-Mile E-Commerce Tax
paragraphs: Walk onto a contract factory floor in Vietnam, and you immediately understand why Nike's balance sheet looks so light. Nike owns zero footwear factories. Instead, independent manufacturers across 11 countries build 100% of NIKE Brand footwear, with just four major manufacturing groups supplying roughly 60% of total pairs and three nations—Vietnam at 52%, Indonesia at 27%, and China at 16%—accounting for 95% of volume. Apparel follows the same outsourced blueprint across Vietnam, China, and Cambodia. Because those partners absorb the heavy plant and machinery depreciation, Nike spent just $684 million on capital expenditures in FY2026—a remarkably slim 1.5% of revenue.

So why did margins erode when Nike tried to push 50% of sales through digital channels under Consumer Direct Acceleration? Because the savings at the factory gate got eaten alive at the customer's front door. On a spreadsheet, selling a $140 sneaker on Nike.com instead of wholesale to Dick's Sporting Goods at ~$75 looks like an instant gross-margin windfall. In the real world, single-parcel shipping, reverse logistics on free returns, paid digital acquisition, and outlet markdowns pile heavy variable costs into Cost of Sales and Operating Overhead—while abandoning roughly half of wholesale accounts choked off organic shopper discovery. Under Elliott Hill's 'Win Now' course correction, Wholesale climbed back to $27,515 million in FY2026, or ~59% of consolidated revenue, while NIKE Direct stepped down to $17,692 million, or ~38%. That deliberate detox continued in Q1 FY2027, where NIKE Brand Wholesale held at $6.8 billion and jumped 9% in North America while NIKE Direct dropped 8% to $4.14 billion, led by a 13% pullback in Digital and a 5% decline in owned stores.

book_subsections.title: Anatomy of a $100 Nike Sale: From Cost of Sales to Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: Let us trace a single $100 bill across Nike's audited FY2026 income statement so you can see exactly where the profit leaks and why management launched 'Pace.' Out of every $100 of consolidated revenue—$46,398 million in total—Cost of Sales consumed $57.09, covering factory product cost, ocean freight, duties, and warehousing, leaving $42.91 in gross profit, or a 42.9% gross margin. Next, Demand Creation—the global campaigns, NBA and NFL kit rights, and athlete endorsements totaling $4,754 million—took $10.25. Operating Overhead, encompassing corporate payroll, retail store leases, IT, and logistics totaling $11,360 million including $747 million of depreciation, absorbed another $24.48.

Do that subtraction with me: $42.91 minus $10.25 minus $24.48 leaves just $8.18 in operating profit per $100 of sales, or $3,797 million total. After $103 million in net interest and other non-operating income and $792 million in taxes, Net Income landed at $3,108 million, or $6.70 per $100 of revenue. Yet working-capital drag compressed Operating Cash Flow to $2,868 million, and after $684 million in CapEx, Free Cash Flow shrank to $2,184 million—just $4.71 out of every $100 sold, falling short of the $2,407 million paid in dividends. That 4.7% free-cash-flow margin is the exact arithmetic that pushed Hill and CFO Dave Denton to target $2.5 billion in annualized run-rate 'Pace' savings through FY2031.
